title: Scaler Cofounder Anshuman Singh Launches Arcfront, an AI Training Data Venture
excerpt: Arcfront sells ‘Decision Arc Data’ — records of how experts reach decisions — to frontier AI labs; Singh says four of the five labs signed on within a year.
body:
• Scaler cofounder Anshuman Singh has launched Arcfront, a venture that turns records of how experts make decisions into training data, reinforcement-learning environments and evaluations for frontier AI labs.
  • Singh says four of the five frontier AI labs became Arcfront customers in under a year; he has not named the labs, and the claim is the company's own.
  • He is building Arcfront with Naman Bhalla, Scaler's former head of AI products and an ex-Google engineer, with support from Scaler cofounder Abhimanyu Saxena.
  • The venture operates under Evaratus Inc., identified in recruitment material as formerly Scaler AI Labs; its current ownership relationship with Scaler is unconfirmed.

Anshuman Singh, cofounder of the tech upskilling platform Scaler, has unveiled Arcfront, an AI research and training data venture built on a simple observation: models that can solve hard coding and mathematics problems still struggle with the judgement calls that professional work requires. Arcfront reconstructs how experts reach decisions — the options they reject, the revisions they make, the outcomes that follow — and converts those records into training material for advanced AI models, Inc42 reported.

Singh is building the venture with Naman Bhalla, Scaler's former head of AI products and an ex-Google software engineer, and said Arcfront has “deep support” from Scaler cofounder Abhimanyu Saxena. In his launch post, Singh wrote: “We spent ten years building a school for software engineers. Now we build one for models,” and put the operation at more than 300 enterprise partners and over 1,000 reinforcement-learning environments. The company is hiring in San Francisco and Bengaluru.

‘Decision Arc Data’

Arcfront calls its approach “Decision Arc Data.” The records it builds become training data, reinforcement-learning environments — settings in which models practise tasks and receive feedback — and evaluations for frontier labs. Its work covers software engineering, site reliability engineering, cybersecurity and collaborative workplace tasks, and it builds sector-specific evaluations using workflows from healthcare, life sciences, legal services and finance to find where models fail, according to Inc42.

Singh claimed that four of the five frontier AI labs became Arcfront's customers within less than a year of operations. He did not identify the labs. Separately, angel investor Gokul Rajaram identified Arcfront as the company behind his earlier claim about a startup reaching a $1 billion annualised revenue run rate faster than any other company; in that earlier post, Rajaram said the unnamed company had no revenue in November 2025 and generated $80 million in September 2026. Arcfront has not publicly confirmed those revenue figures.

What is still unclear

Arcfront operates under Evaratus Inc., according to its website's legal disclosures, and company recruitment material identifies Evaratus as formerly Scaler AI Labs, Scaler's frontier AI research and engineering division. The public disclosures reviewed by Inc42 do not establish Evaratus's current shareholding or whether the business has been separated from the Scaler group, and Inc42 said it has sought clarity from the founders. Singh's LinkedIn profile lists November 2025 as the end of his tenure at Scaler and the start of his work on Arcfront.

Part of a crowded data race

Arcfront enters a market that Indian founders are contesting from several directions. Bengaluru's Humyn Labs raised $47 million this week to collect real-world data for training robots, and Deccan AI raised $25 million in March for post-training data and enterprise infrastructure. The difference is the raw material: where others record people performing physical or digital tasks, Arcfront is selling the record of expert judgement itself.
